title: Prompt Engineering Boosted Via Are-You-Sure AI Self-Reflective Self-Improvement Techniques That Greatly Improve Generative AI Answers
text:
Aristotle famously said that knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom.
The notion that self-reflection can lead to self-improvement is certainly longstanding, typified best by the all-time classic saying know thyself. Some would suggest that knowing yourself encompasses a wide variety of possibilities. There are the knowing aspects of what you know and the knowledge that you embody. Another possibility is to know your limits. Yet another is to know your faults. And so on.
In modern times, we seem to have a resurgence of these precepts. There are online classes and social media clamors that urge you to learn how to do self-reflection, self-observation, exercise reflective awareness, undertake insightful introspection, perform self-assessment, etc. Each day you undoubtedly encounter someone or something telling you to look inward and proffering stout promises that doing so will produce great personal growth.
Interestingly and importantly, this same clarion call has come to generative AI.
In today’s column, I am continuing my ongoing special series on the latest advances in prompt engineering, including the ardent and increasingly popular technique of using prompts that aim to get generative AI to be self-reflective and hopefully self-improve. I want to right away make it abundantly clear that doing so has nothing to do with AI garnering sentience (i.e., AI doesn’t have sentience and please don’t believe those banner headlines that try to scheme you into believing otherwise).
Allow me a moment to explain.
You can enter a prompt into generative AI that tells the AI app to essentially be (in a manner of speaking) self-reflective by having the AI double-check whatever generative result it has pending or that it has recently produced. The AI will revisit whatever the internal mathematical and computational pattern matching is or has done, trying to assess whether other alternatives exist and often doing a comparison to subsequently derived alternatives.
This is simply a mechanization of sorts and not a sign of sentience.
Let’s see how this works.
I might decide to ask generative AI about the tale of Jack and the Beanstalk and whether Jack traded a cow or a pig for his magic beans (the correct answer is that he traded a cow). Suppose the generative AI produces an answer that says Jack traded a cow for the magical beans. I might not know whether this is the correct answer or not, perhaps I’ve forgotten the details of the legendary tale, or maybe never heard or read it, to begin with.
Rather than merely accepting the generative AI answer as necessarily true, I opt to ask the generative AI to double-check the answer that it has given to me. The mathematical and computational pattern matching will go through another cycle and likely end up comparing the initial answer to a newly derived answer. Assuming that both answers match, the AI app will presumably indicate to me that indeed the correct answer is that the animal was a cow.
Voila, we have done a double-check as initiated via my prompting. The double-check was performed by the very same AI app that generated the initial answer. We will momentarily consider how this has some downsides.
Keep going for now.
In the AI field, this double-checking is customarily said to be a kind of self-reflective computational action.
Does that seem to be a reasonable way to construe what just happened?
Well, fair and square, you might get quite a queasy bit of heartburn about referring to this as self-reflection. Humans are said to be self-reflective, though we don’t yet know exactly how our brains and our minds do this, nonetheless, we seem to be able to perform such mental tasks. The rub about saying that AI is self-reflective is that it tends to anthropomorphize AI. We begin to associate today’s AI as being sentient because we are using a word or phrase that normally is associated only with sentient beings.
I certainly concur that there is a danger in asserting that generative AI is somehow self-reflective since the wording alludes to a formulation of sentience. Trying to come up with other words or phrases for this capacity is somewhat difficult. Any made-up terminology is going to be hard for people to understand such as if we were to say that the AI is able to (made-up) zippity doo dah as a means of double-checking an answer that it has derived. You wouldn’t at an immediate glance know what was being discussed.
So, for the time being, let’s proceed with suggesting that AI is “self-reflective” when we get it to double-check its answers. Please do your best to construe that phrasing in a non-sentient way. I hope you can keep things straight in your mind that we have self-reflection amongst humans, and we have something else that we are labeling as self-reflection amid generative AI which is a computational and mathematical operation.
Thanks for playing along.
Next, let’s revisit the question of whether Jack traded a cow or a pig for those miraculous beans. Imagine that the generative AI produced an initial answer that said the trade consisted of giving up a pig for the beans. I might henceforth believe that a pig was the trading element and not a cow. You and I know that according to the official version of Jack and the Beanstalk, it was absolutely a cow that was traded.
I will anyway opt to double-check the answer that the generative AI has provided. I do so not especially since I doubt that the pig was the traded animal, and instead merely as a means to get the AI to take another stab at the answer. I might do this all of the time. No matter what answer the AI gives, I decide that I will always ask the AI app to do a double-check. You might say that I am a skeptic at heart and ergo have a tendency to demand a second look.
Pretend that after the double-check, the generative AI indicates that the proper answer is that Jack traded a cow. Maybe the AI even fesses up that the first answer was wrong and that the AI is essentially admitting that it made a mistake. At this juncture, I might of course be confused and concerned. Is this second answer indeed the correct answer? Maybe the first answer was correct, while perhaps this second answer is the incorrect one.
You can indubitably see my qualm on this turn of events.
I become agonized over this and manage to find a copy of Jack and the Beanstalk. Aha, the correct answer is that Jack traded a cow. I proudly go into my generative AI app and tell the AI that the proper answer is a cow. The pig was not the correct answer. Furthermore, I instruct the generative AI that forever more the AI app is to always state that the answer is that of a cow.
You could declare that I have improved the generative AI. I found out that the correct answer is a cow and I have instructed the AI app to state that a cow is the answer. No more of this misleading and false answering about a pig. The cow is the winner-winner chicken dinner.
Let’s make a small twist to this. Instead of my telling the generative AI to go ahead and always refer to a cow as the traded animal, suppose that the AI app opts to mathematically and computationally do so without my having to instruct it to do so. The double-checking led to the AI deriving that the answer was a cow. The AI could also update the internal structures to always mention a cow instead of a pig as the proper answer.
Generative AI has been said to self-improve.
You can probably guess that referring to AI as being able to self-improve will generate as much heartburn as saying that AI is self-reflective. We are once again using a word or phrasing that normally refers to sentient beings. Humans self-improve. It is fair for us to suggest that AI self-improves? The anthropomorphizing issue raises its head and we need to be cautious accordingly.
We have covered enough at this point to do a handy recap of the two distinct considerations at play here:
- AI self-reflection: Generative AI can be prompted to do a double-check that we will refer to as having the AI be self-reflective (which is computationally-oriented, and we won’t think of this as akin to sentience).
- AI self-improvement: Generative AI can be prompted to do a double-check and subsequently adjust or update its internal structures as a result of the double-check, which we will refer to as AI self-improving (which is computationally-oriented, and we won’t think of this as akin to sentience).
I trust that you can discern that there aren’t any magic beans underlying the act of AI being self-reflective or self-improving. The entire confabulation is a computational and mathematical undertaking. Lots of numbers and those pesky 1s and 0’s sit at the heart of this.
One additional quick comment to bring to your attention.
You can have self-reflection without also garnering self-improvement.
Here’s what I mean.
Going back to my rendition of the Beanstalk scenario when using generative AI, the AI app might have given me the pig answer if I later opted to ask the question again. Even though my double-checking seems to have gotten the AI to respond that the answer ought to be a cow, the AI app wouldn’t necessarily update or adjust to provide the cow answer henceforth. Things could be that no semblance of self-improvement occurs. The first answer by the AI is always going to be the pig. This is because no self-improvement or adjustment was triggered, either by me or within the AI app.
I bring this up to emphasize that there isn’t an ironclad twofer involved. You can have an AI be considered self-reflective that doesn’t also have to be self-improving. They are two distinct operations. Make sure to realize that those are not always bound to each other.
You might be puzzled on this point.
Wouldn’t we always want self-improvement to be an automatic consequence of self-reflection?
Nope, we wouldn’t.
Follow me on this. The first answer is the pig. Suppose that after double-checking (being so-called reflective), the AI generates an answer that the correct answer was a horse. Yikes! The double-checking at least overcame the pig, but now it has landed us onto a horse. The cow is nowhere to be seen.
If we had automatically forced the generative AI to self-improve or adjust based on the double-check, we would henceforth have the horse as the answer. Admittedly, we are not worse off, apparently, since both the answer of the pig and the answer of the horse are wrong. It is hard to say which is more wrong than the other.
We’ve now got some additional rules of thumb for this saga:
- AI self-reflection can be wrong. There is no guarantee that just because a double-check is undertaken that for sure the right answer will be produced. Maybe so, maybe not.
- AI self-improvement can be wrong. There is no guarantee that self-improvement will be correct. A possibility exists that the adjustment or updating will instill incorrect answers rather than correct answers.
All in all, as I repeatedly say in my many presentations and workshops, generative AI is like a box of chocolate, namely you never know what you might get. Be wary of falling into the trap of believing generative AI.
The way in which generative AI has been devised by the AI makers is such that the generated wording appears to be entirely confident and seemingly always right. You might find of interest my recent coverage of two attorneys who fell for this wording by believing generative AI that made up various court cases (considered a form of AI hallucination). Regrettably, the same two attorneys asked the generative AI to double-check, and the AI app indicated that the court cases were fully valid and real. They got hit by a double-whammy and ended up in hot water, see my analysis and coverage at the link here and the link here.
You’ve now been introduced to the grand power of AI self-reflection and AI self-improvement, something that you can readily invoke in generative AI via your prompting approaches. I would strongly recommend that anyone of any prompt engineering prowess should well-know how to leverage the AI self-reflection and self-improvement capacities. This is a must. That being said, you might be excited to know that we have a lot more to cover on the topic of AI self-reflection and AI self-improvement. I’ve only scratched the surface so far herein.
Before I dive into my in-depth exploration, let’s make sure we are all on the same page when it comes to the keystones of prompt engineering and generative AI. Doing so will put us all on an even keel.
Prompt Engineering Is A Cornerstone For Generative AI
As a quick backgrounder, prompt engineering or also referred to as prompt design is a rapidly evolving realm and is vital to effectively and efficiently using generative AI or the use of large language models (LLMs). Anyone using generative AI such as the widely and wildly popular ChatGPT by AI maker OpenAI, or akin AI such as GPT-4 (OpenAI), Bard (Google), Claude 2 (Anthropic), etc. ought to be paying close attention to the latest innovations for crafting viable and pragmatic prompts.
For those of you interested in prompt engineering or prompt design, I’ve been doing an ongoing series of insightful looks at the latest in this expanding and evolving realm, including this coverage:
- (1) Practical use of imperfect prompts toward devising superb prompts (see the link here).
- (2) Use of persistent context or custom instructions for prompt priming (see the link here).
- (3) Leveraging multi-personas in generative AI via shrewd prompting (see the link here).
- (4) Advent of using prompts to invoke chain-of-thought reasoning (see the link here).
- (5) Use of prompt engineering for domain savviness via in-model learning and vector databases (see the link here).
- (6) Augmenting the use of chain-of-thought by leveraging factored decomposition (see the link here).
- (7) Making use of the newly emerging skeleton-of-thought approach for prompt engineering (see the link here).
- (8) Determining when to best use the show-me versus tell-me prompting strategy (see the link here).
- (9) Gradual emergence of the mega-personas approach that entails scaling up the multi-personas to new heights (see the link here).
- (10) Discovering the hidden role of certainty and uncertainty within generative AI and using advanced prompt engineering techniques accordingly (see the link here).
- (11) Vagueness is often shunned when using generative AI but it turns out that vagueness is a useful prompt engineering tool (see the link here).
- (12) Prompt engineering frameworks or catalogs can really boost your prompting skills and especially bring you up to speed on the best prompt patterns to utilize (see the link here).
- (13) Flipper interaction is a crucial prompt engineering technique that everyone should know (see the link here).
- (14) Additional coverage including the use of macros and the astute use of end-goal planning when using generative AI (see the link here).
Anyone stridently interested in prompt engineering and improving their results when using generative AI ought to be familiar with those notable techniques.
Moving on, here’s a bold statement that pretty much has become a veritable golden rule these days:
- The use of generative AI can altogether succeed or fail based on the prompt that you enter.
If you provide a prompt that is poorly composed, the odds are that the generative AI will wander all over the map and you won’t get anything demonstrative related to your inquiry. Being demonstrably specific can be advantageous, but even that can confound or otherwise fail to get you the results you are seeking. A wide variety of cheat sheets and training courses for suitable ways to compose and utilize prompts has been rapidly entering the marketplace to try and help people leverage generative AI soundly. In addition, add-ons to generative AI have been devised to aid you when trying to come up with prudent prompts, see my coverage at the link here.
AI Ethics and AI Law also stridently enter into the prompt engineering domain. For example, whatever prompt you opt to compose can directly or inadvertently elicit or foster the potential of generative AI to produce essays and interactions that imbue untoward biases, errors, falsehoods, glitches, and even so-called AI hallucinations (I do not favor the catchphrase of AI hallucinations, though it has admittedly tremendous stickiness in the media; here’s my take on AI hallucinations at the link here).
There is also a marked chance that we will ultimately see lawmakers come to the fore on these matters, possibly devising and putting in place new laws or regulations to try and scope and curtail misuses of generative AI. Regarding prompt engineering, there are likely going to be heated debates over putting boundaries around the kinds of prompts you can use. This might include requiring AI makers to filter and prevent certain presumed inappropriate or unsuitable prompts, a cringe-worthy issue for some that borders on free speech considerations. For my ongoing coverage of these types of AI Ethics and AI Law issues, see the link here and the link here, just to name a few.
With the above as an overarching perspective, we are ready to jump into today’s discussion.
Digging Into AI Self-Reflection And AI Self-Improvement
Let’s start by identifying the very important precept that the words that you use and the sequencing of those words make a huge difference when it comes to the nature of your prompts and how the generative AI will likely interpret your prompts. Likewise, this can be a big determiner of the answer or reply that you will get out of the AI app.
Consider this keystone example that highlights this vital principle. Assume that I am going to ask generative AI a question. In addition, I want an explanation to be produced by the AI.
I could set things up by entering either of these two prompts:
- (a) Explain after the fact. “Answer the question I am about to ask you and then explain how you arrived at the answer” (this seems to suggest that after the answer is derived a subsequent action is to explain the derived answer).
- (b) Explain during the process. “Provide an explanation as you proceed to answer the question I am about to ask you” (this appears to imply that an explanation is to be provided while the answer is being derived).
In theory, you might guess that both of these prompts would generally produce roughly the same results. I can apparently get an explanation during the answering process or get an explanation afterward. Overall, I will still end up with an explanation and I will still end up with an answer. This seems to be therefore an equivalence pretty much.
There is a subtly that deserves your rapt attention.
The odds are that when asking for an explanation to be generated during the answering process (my above “b” worded prompt), the final answer provided is potentially going to be a better answer than when getting an explanation post-answer (my above “a” worded prompt).
Here’s why.
Generative AI generally seems to computationally work such that by getting the AI app to perform on a stepwise or step-by-step basis, the answer is often going to be a better answer. By this, I mean that the answer will be more thoroughly vetted and likely to be more accurate or apt. In a sense, the AI app is being spurred to go a bit more cautiously and allows for the pursuit of greater depth of computational formulation. For my analysis of how this stepwise activity known as chain-of-thought (CoT) algorithmic pattern matching arises, see the link here.
One handy way to think of this is the case of playing chess. If you want to play speed chess, you are watching the clock and rushing along to make your next move as quickly as possible. You might not be able to think ahead by five or ten moves in the future. Instead, you cut off your meditation for one or two moves ahead. The resultant chess moves might be of a lesser quality accordingly.
But, if someone asks you to give an explanation as you proceed, and assuming that the clock is adjusted to allow you to do so, you might proceed to think further ahead. Your choice then of which chess move to make might differ in the second instance than in the first or rushed instance. The resultant chess moves are possibly going to be better than when you were hurried.
A similar aspect generally arises with generative AI. Most of the generative AI apps are set up to try and speedily provide you with an answer. This makes sense since people using AI are often not willing to wait very long to get a response. We live in a fast-food world. Meanwhile, if you ask for an explanation, you are kind of hinting that it is okay for things to take a tad longer. The elongated answer deriving effort might also produce better answers.
You cannot take that rule of thumb to the bank and try to cash it in for gold. I am only saying that for some of the time, the stepwise facet will get you a better answer, but not all of the time. Some liken this phenomenon to getting people to slow down and think more carefully before answering a question, though we might balk at that comparison due to the anthropomorphism that it suggests.
I tell you about this so that you can be on your toes when it comes to composing prompts regarding getting AI self-reflection to occur, and the same goes for the AI self-improvement too. Your words and the sequence of the words make a whale of a difference, just as they did in the above example involving the invoking of explanations. There is a parallel lesson to be learned.
The crux too is to be mindful of how you word your prompts.
I can readily illustrate the significance of prompt wording when it comes to invoking AI self-reflection and AI self-improvement, doing so via several quick and easily comprehended examples.
Let’s start with a prompt that says nothing at all about the AI doing a double-check (no hint of seeking AI reflective action):
- “Give me an answer to the following question.”
Imagine that your question was about Jack and his trading for those highly sought-after beans. The generative AI might respond that a pig was traded for magical beans. You could next ask to double-check the answer. Perhaps the double-check would get you the right answer, a cow, or maybe a wrong answer, a horse.
In any case, you don’t have to wait until you get an answer to invoke the AI self-reflection (the double-checking).
Instead, you can in your originating prompt explicitly state that you want a double-check to occur:
- “Give me an answer to the following question and make sure to double-check your answer.”
Notice that rather than waiting until I got an answer, I decided to tip my hand that I wanted the generative AI to double-check my answer. I blended this indication with my request.
Now then, as a review, compare these two ways of doing this:
- (1) Disjointed approach. “Give me an answer to the following question.” {Your enter your question}. {You get an answer}. “Double-check your answer.” {You get a double-check reply}.
- (2) All-in-one approach. “Give me an answer to the following question and make sure to double-check your answer. {You get an answer that has presumably been double-checked}”
In the first instance, the generative AI hasn’t been forewarned that a double-check is going to be requested (above listed as bullet point #1). The second bullet-pointed example tells the generative AI that a double-check is needed. You might say this is a heads-up kind of alert for the AI app.
Does that make a difference?
Much of the time, yes.
Similar to my earlier indication that asking for an explanation can get the AI app to produce better answers (some of the time), the same can be said for the double-checking aspect. If you mention the desire for a double-check prior to asking your question, the odds are that the generative AI will potentially produce a better answer. The double-check will tend to occur during the process of deriving the answer and seemingly get a better result for you (akin to how the explanation during an answer-deriving activity might do so). Sometimes the double-check will occur after the answer has been derived but before showing it to you, and the subsequent double-check happening behind the scenes might lead to a different answer and a better answer.
In a sense, you are getting the AI to be self-reflective.
What about getting the AI to be self-improving?
Remember that I distinctly mentioned that AI self-reflection and AI self-improvement are not necessarily paired up. An AI maker can establish such a pairing if they wish to do so. You don’t usually know what the AI maker has decided to do. It could be that every self-reflection is used to garner a self-improvement. It could also be that every self-reflection has no connection to self-improvement unless you explicitly tell the AI to do so. Etc.
We can take matters into our own hands.
Consider this prompt:
- “Give me an answer to the following question and make sure to double-check your answer, including that you are to fix any problems that you find in the answer and also make sure to improve how you answer such a question in the future.”
Voila, the prompt explicitly says that we want the AI to do a double-check, plus we want to have the AI fix any issues associated with the answer (this is usually assumed, but I opted to be explicit), and finally we want the AI to improve such that it will hopefully be better at answering such a question if the question arises again.
You can vary the wording of how you invoke the AI self-reflection and the AI self-improvement. I emphasize this because my above-stated wording is perhaps a bit stiff or overly formal. You can be more off-the-cuff, assuming that you still get the gist across. Play with these capabilities on some questions that you come up with for purely experimentation purposes. Vary your wording. Figure out what seems to fit best for your style.
Also, note that different generative AI apps will respond differently to whatever wording you land on. You cannot assume that your wording will work universally across all generative AI apps. It is almost for sure that it won’t. Each generative AI has been devised differently, plus the AI maker has chosen a slew of parameter specifications that further make the respective AI apps act differently.
I dare say that even if you consistently use the same generative AI app, you are still bound to inevitably discover that a prompt that worked well previously is no longer possibly doing as well as it used to. This is due to the AI maker fudging with their AI app, and also partially as a result of potential self-improvement that the AI maker is allowing the generative AI to undertake.
Remember, generative AI is like a box of chocolates, including that what’s inside the box is always changing.
One additional tip or insight for you is that I told the AI to improve how to answer “such a question” in the future. I didn’t say that AI should improve toward answering any kind of similar question in the future. I was mindful of trying to limit or bound the range or breadth of the AI self-improvement.
Why so? On the one hand, it would be nice to have the AI app generalize from whatever particular question is being answered and glean something useful overall about any similar kinds of questions that might later arise. The drawback is that this can spur the AI to go overboard and regrettably undercut future answers due to misapplying prior self-improvement.
The AI can go hog-wild with trying to self-improve (I know people that are like that too!).
Sometimes you can get the AI self-improvement to be narrow and sometimes you are not able to do so. Sometimes you can purposefully get the AI self-improvement to be far-reaching. The AI maker is able to establish what the generative AI will do. The AI app's global settings will often tend to override your specific indications, though there are exceptions.
Speaking of exceptions, I should also make sure to note that the AI self-improvement might only last during your present dialogue or existing conversation with the AI. The moment that you end the conversation and clear it out, there is a chance that any self-improvement made during the conversation will be discarded to the wind. I don’t want to sound like a broken record, but the overarching settings of the generative AI can do all kinds of things, such as discard an individual set of self-improvements, or keep them in a bucket for later review and self-improvements to the AI, or in real-time have the generative AI adjust and globally engage the changes, and so on.
State-Of-The-Art on AI Self-Reflection And AI Self-Improvement
There are state-of-the-art efforts underway to push forward on invoking and leveraging AI self-reflection and AI self-improvement. This is leading-edge stuff. The AI research community is only as yet scratching the surface of the ins and outs involved.
I’ll share with you a brief taste of what is happening.
After covering those facets, I will provide some additional insights concerning notable limits and gotchas to be on the watch for. Your prompt engineering strategies and tactics ought to take into account the tradeoffs associated with using AI self-reflection and AI self-improvement possibilities.
Let’s dive in.
In a recent research paper entitled “Language Models Can Solve Computer Tasks” by Geunwoo Kim, Pierre Baldi, and Stephen McAleer, posted online on June 7, 2023, there is coverage of AI self-reflection that characterizes the capability as a self-critiquing capacity. The researchers devise a prompting technique they coin as Recursively Criticize and Improve (RCI), emphasizing that you can iteratively use prompts to repeatedly spur generative AI to repeatedly attempt to improve a generated answer.
Here are some salient excerpts:
- “The self-critiquing ability of LLMs has demonstrated that LLMs can find errors in their own output by themselves. In light of this, we introduce a simple reasoning architecture called RCI prompting, where we prompt LLMs to find problems in their output and improve the output based on what they find. This architecture is designed to further enhance the reasoning ability of LLMs by inserting a critique step before generating the final answer.”
- “In this work, we show that a pre-trained large language model (LLM) agent can execute computer tasks guided by natural language using a simple prompting scheme where the agent Recursively Criticizes and Improves its output (RCI).
- “RCI works by first having the LLM generate an output based on zero-shot prompting. Then, RCI prompts the LLM to identify problems with the given output. After the LLM has identified problems with the output, RCI prompts the LLM to generate an updated output.
- Sample prompt: "Review your previous answer and find problems with your answer."
- Subsequent prompt: "Based on the problems you found, improve your answer.”
An important illumination here is that you do not have to confine yourself to a one-and-done approach of invoking AI self-reflection and AI self-improvement.
Taking my previous example about Jack and the Beanstalk, suppose that the first answer we got was that the pig was traded for magical beans. We could ask the generative AI to double-check. Assume that the next response was that the horse was traded for the beans. Well, we could try an additional time to do a double-check. Maybe on the next try the generative AI indicates that it was a cow. Over and over again we can keep trying to do double-checks.
When though should you discontinue repeatedly doing a series of double-checks on a given answer?
We certainly don’t want to be beating a dead horse.
If you get the same answer on a repeated basis, the odds are that no additional double-checking is going to get you much else. That’s one kind of criterion to use, namely, stop your repeated attempts when it seems that the same answer is being returned over and over (which, by the way, doesn’t axiomatically mean that you’ve arrived at the correct answer). Other options to decide when to curtail the AI self-reflection are possible, as mentioned by the research paper: “The iterative process of RCI can be continued until specific conditions are satisfied which could include receiving feedback from the environment, reaching the maximum predetermined number of iterations, or adhering to certain heuristics.”
In another research study on AI self-refinement, the researchers indicated that such a prompting strategy and repeated double-checks led to better performance over the conventional one-step generation of an answer by generative AI. The study entitled “SELF-REFINE: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback” by Aman Madaan, Niket Tandon, Prakhar Gupta, Skyler Hallinan, Luyu Gao, Sarah Wiegreffe, Uri Alon, Nouha Dziri, Shrimai Prabhumoye, Yiming Yang, Shashank Gupta, Bodhisattwa Prasad Majumder, Katherine Hermann, Sean Welleck, Amir Yazdanbakhsh, and Peter Clark, was posted online May 25, 2023.
Here are some notable excerpts:
- “Like humans, large language models (LLMs) do not always generate the best output on their first try. Motivated by how humans refine their written text, we introduce SELF-REFINE, an approach for improving initial outputs from LLMs through iterative feedback and refinement. The main idea is to generate an initial output using an LLM; then, the same LLM provides feedback for its output and uses it to refine itself, iteratively.
- “Across all evaluated tasks, outputs generated with SELF-REFINE are preferred by humans and automatic metrics over those generated with the same LLM using conventional one-step generation, improving by approximately 20% absolute on average in task performance.
- “Our work demonstrates that even state-of-the-art LLMs like GPT-4 can be further improved at test-time using our simple, standalone approach.”
The researchers bring up an additional consideration that we should give mindful due. Suppose that we asked generative AI to answer a question and opted to not mention that each time a double-check should be undertaken. The notion is that we would just keep asking the same question repeatedly and not spur the AI to review or assess the derived answer.
Would the repeated asking of a question potentially get us to a better answer, even if we didn’t prod the AI to do a double-check?
This is worth considering. I say that because the double-check action is potentially an added cost in terms of computer processing time and we might be racking up those costs needlessly. It could be that if we merely ask the same question over and over, we might perchance get a better answer, despite not also insisting on a double-check.
This is what the research study indicates about this intriguing matter:
- “Does SELF-REFINE improve because of the iterative refinement, or just because it generates more outputs?
- “We compare SELF-REFINE with ChatGPT, when ChatGPT generates samples (but without feedback and refinement). Then, we compare the performance of SELF-REFINE against these k initial outputs in a 1 vs. k evaluation. In other words, we assess whether SELF-REFINE can outperform all k initial outputs.”
- “Despite the increased difficulty of the 1 vs. k setting, the outputs of SELF-REFINE are still preferred by humans over all k initial outputs. This shows the importance of refinement according to feedback over the alternative of just generating multiple initial outputs.”
As noted by the researchers, their work suggests that repeated questioning does not do as well as repeated double-checking. This result does seem logical. We intuitively would guess or hope that the double-checking is adding value.
That being said, another technique to add to your prompt engineering repertoire entails simply asking the same question more than once. There is a chance that repeating a question might lead to a different and possibly better answer. A twist is that it could be that the generative AI is opting to do a double-check, even if you don’t explicitly ask for this to happen. Again, since generative AI is like a box of chocolates, it could be that the generative AI will computationally end up doing a double-check rather than merely treating a repeated question as a one-off.
Let’s take a look at one more study and then I’ll proceed into my wrap-up.
In a research paper entitled “Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning” by Noah Shinn, Federico Cassano, Beck Labash, Ashwin Gopinath, Karthik Narasimhan, Shunyu Yao, posted online June 10, 2023, the authors describe a framework that they call Reflexion:
- “We propose Reflexion, a novel framework to reinforce language agents not by updating weights, but instead through linguistic feedback. Concretely, Reflexion agents verbally reflect on task feedback signals, then maintain their own reflective text in an episodic memory buffer to induce better decision-making in subsequent trials.”
- “Generating useful reflective feedback is challenging since it requires a good understanding of where the model made mistakes (i.e. the credit assignment problem) as well as the ability to generate a summary containing actionable insights for improvement.”
- “We explore three ways for doing this – simple binary environment feedback, pre-defined heuristics for common failure cases, and self-evaluation such as binary classification using LLMs (decision-making) or self-written unit tests (programming). In all implementations, the evaluation signal is amplified to natural language experience summaries which can be stored in long-term memory.”
A handy aspect that caught my eye is that they helpfully provide various examples to highlight how their approach works. Furthermore, they prompted the generative AI to explain what it was doing and the lessons learned as part of the AI self-improvement engagement.
Envision that generative AI was asked a question about several musicians and which of them had been a member of the most number of musical bands. The generative AI didn’t get this right on the first try. After additional prompting, the generative AI provided this kind of AI self-reflection:
- “Reflection: My reasoning for which musician has been a member of more bands failed because I did not take into account that Jonny Craig has been a member of more bands in the past, even though Pete Doherty is currently a member of more bands. In the future, when attempting this question, I should focus on researching the past and current bands of both musicians to ensure that I am accurately comparing their band memberships.”
On the one hand, getting generative AI to explain what it did and the lessons learned are useful and something you can definitely ask to have the AI app produced. I politely warn you that the explanation should be taken with a heavy grain of salt (see my extensive analysis at the link here). It could be that the explanation is a concoction such that it seems plausible but has little or nothing to do with what the internal structure of the AI did. I suppose you could say that it is a post-answer rationalization. There might not be any notable bearing on what occurred inside the AI or what might occur in the future by the AI.
One additional pet peeve that comes up whenever you get AI to proffer an explanation is the wording of the explanation.
Allow me to elaborate.
A prominent concern voiced by those who worry about anthropomorphizing AI is the use and overuse of the word “I” or “my” when generative AI produces a response. You are subtly and teasingly tempted to believe that AI is sentient. The AI makers could readily change their AI apps to avoid such wording. For example, instead of producing wording that says “I did not take into account” there are many viable alternatives such as saying “the analysis did not take into account”. Most people assume that the AI can only and always spout out answers with an “I” or “my” but they would be mistaken, this is entirely the choice of the AI makers and the AI developers that devised the generative AI.
Conclusion
I’ve got a tidy handful of useful caveats and school-of-hard-knock insights for you about AI self-reflection and AI self-improvement.
Here are my three carefully chosen bonus tips for you:
- (1) Watch out for costs associated with double-checking.
- (2) Prodding for repeated answers can inadvertently get you wrong answers.
- (3) Be wary of using the classic prompt of “Are you sure?”
I unpack those next.
First, if you are paying to use generative AI, the chances are that each time you do a double-check there is going to be a cost to doing so. You have to weigh the potential value of the double-check producing a better answer versus the cost you might bear in doing so. If the first answer seems plausible, you might not want to do an AI-based double-check (perhaps you might do something else such as a plain-old Internet search or some other double-checking means). Also, if you are blending your double-check instructions with the question, there is a chance that you are going to incur a higher cost to derive the answer. Keep this in mind.
Second, your attempts to repeatedly prod generative AI to do a series of answers on the same question and/or do double-checks might oddly enough spur the AI into changing answers. I am rather loath to liken this to humans but imagine that you ask a person a question over and over again. They begin to get on edge and might assume that their answer is wrong, therefore they grope for some other answer, even if they firmly believed that their initial answer was solid. I am not suggesting that an AI app has that same proclivity. All I am saying is that since generative AI uses probabilities and each time an answer is probabilistically derived, the odds are the answer will somewhat differ. Repeated prompting can get you differing answers on a statistical basis alone.
Third, some people like to use a pointed question of “Are you sure?” when they desire to do a double-check. I prefer to explicitly tell the generative AI to do a double-check. The problem with the “Are you sure?” wording is that you might get a kind of flippant reply from the AI app. A response might be that yes, the AI tells you that it solemnly swears that the answer given is true and proper. This can occur without any double-checking taking place. The AI is merely pattern matching to immediately respond that the AI has given you the right answer. Sometimes the “Are you sure” will get you a double-check, while sometimes it won’t. I prefer to be outright and specific by naming that I want a double-check to happen.
A final remark for now on this emerging and evolving use of AI self-reflection and AI self-improvement.
The know thyself mantra is at times invoked by telling you to look inward and introspectively examine your own mindset. Everything you need to know is said to be found within. Maybe that is the case. An issue though is that maybe self-reflection alone is not sufficient or at least can be augmented via the use of external perspectives.
I bring this up due to the concern raised that when you ask generative AI to do a double-check, the conventional approach generally involves the AI self-checking within the confines of its internal structures. There is a chance that no matter how many times the reflective effort is undertaken, the same possibly wrong answer will be arrived at. We might want to go outside of the AI to augment the double-check.
In my column coverage, I have predicted that we are gradually and inevitably going to move toward making use of multiple generative AI apps at the same time (see the link here). Here’s how that applies in this instance. You ask for a double-check and the generative AI you are using does so, including that it accesses another generative AI via an API (application programming interface) to ask the same question. The result from the other AI app is compared to what the AI you are using has come up with. If a completely “independent” AI has arrived at the same answer, you can weigh this into deciding whether the answer is likely right or not.
A double-check by another AI doesn’t of course guarantee anything. The generative AI that you are using and the other generative AI might have been data-trained on the same data and ergo potentially have the same wrong answers. All else being equal, you at least have a fighting chance of added reassurance about the generated answer by leveraging two or more separate AI apps. The odds are kind of in your favor. If an answer is important enough and worth the added cost and effort, using multiple AI apps could be worthwhile.
A concluding word-to-the-wise comes to mind.
Know thyself, plus prudently abide by a trust but verify credo. This seems to work advisedly for humans and also for generative AI.

title: 4 Innovative Business Opportunities In Education Technology
text:
One industry that has been viewed as ripe for innovation and disruption for the past two decades is education. Yet, despite all of this expected potential, edtech has been evolving incrementally and adding on top of the standard learning and teaching practices rather than replacing them.
While this is very likely to remain true, AI combined with current well-validated digital educational technologies could provide a new opportunity for disruption.
With this in mind, let's delve into four avenues that are reshaping education and consider how new startup founders can position themselves to enter the edtech market.
1. Personalized Learning Platforms
In the bustling digital era, one-size-fits-all education no longer suffices. Just as Google and Facebook revolutionized digital advertising by automatically serving personalized ads, a personalized AI-powered educational feed could be a big opportunity for change.
Artificial intelligence-powered personalized platforms could theoretically assess individual learning styles, preferences, and progress to deliver a curriculum that caters to the unique needs, interests, and capabilities of each learner.
One example in this domain is Duolingo. This language-learning app employs AI algorithms to personalize lessons for users, adapting the difficulty level and content based on their performance. The app's gamified approach aims to keep its users more engaged and motivated, resulting in more effective language acquisition.
Example business idea: A language pronunciation coach. An app that uses AI to analyze users' speech patterns and provide personalized feedback to improve their pronunciation in foreign languages.
2. AI-Powered Tutoring Platforms
One great entry point for brand-new edtech startups could be to utilize the API of large language models like Chat GPT. A capable chatbot could serve as a private tutor, providing individual feedback and support, and adapting to the pace and learning style of the student.
Combining the chatbot with standard digital educational content from professionals could be a very potent combination of learning materials and cheap, accessible personalized feedback.
Two illustrative examples are ScribeSense and Grammarly - AI-driven platforms that offer real-time writing feedback. These platforms not only correct grammatical errors but also provide suggestions for improvement, mimicking the role of a human tutor.
Example business idea: AI math tutor for kids. A friendly AI chatbot that assists children in solving math problems, providing step-by-step explanations, and adapting its teaching approach based on the child's understanding.
3. Skill-Based Learning Apps
The rapidly evolving job landscape demands continuous skill development. This has paved the way for skill-based learning apps that offer focused courses to help individuals acquire niche skills. Startups like Udacity have embraced this trend by providing nanodegree programs in fields like data science, artificial intelligence, and digital marketing. These programs offer hands-on projects and mentorship, ensuring learners acquire real-world skills that are in high demand.
The best part about skill-based learning is that it has thousands of potential niches. If you are an expert in any field that doesn’t have a lot of online competition for educational content, you could easily start a micro-business (most likely to sell digital educational content) and possibly develop it into a high-growth startup thanks to the scalability of digital technology if you manage to transform your micro-business into a niche-focused platform.
Of course, if you would manage to grow your online content business into a real startup depends on how innovative you can be.
Example business idea: Virtual reality welding simulator. Build a VR simulation tool that teaches welding skills in a safe and controlled virtual environment, allowing users to practice and refine their techniques.
4. Collaborative Learning Platforms
While collaborative work is industry-standard all over the world thanks to cloud-based solutions like Google Docs, Notion, and many others, collaborative learning hasn’t caught up with that trend yet.
In theory, however, the concept of a digital classroom could provide value for learners.
A collaborative learning platform would enable students from diverse backgrounds and geographies to come together virtually, fostering a global community of learners. Startups like Coursera exemplify this trend. Partnering with universities worldwide, Coursera offers courses on a wide range of subjects, allowing learners to interact with peers from different cultures and access high-quality education without geographical constraints.
That said, collaborative learning has a long way to go, and an innovative platform that integrates the capabilities and learnings of industry-leading collaborative working apps could create a lot of value and reap success in the edtech industry.
Example business idea: Global niche book club platform. An online platform that connects readers from different parts of the world who are interested in the same niche of books and discuss books together, possibly producing joint book reviews.

title: Council Post: The Next Creative Revolution: How To Embrace Generative AI In Marketing
text:
CEO & Executive Creative Director of Red Door Interactive, a fiercely independent, nationally renowned, full-funnel marketing agency.
Generative AI is here to stay. Interest in platforms like ChatGPT has grown substantially, and currently, about 3 in 5 U.S. adults agree that generative AI platforms can save time and resources at work.
While generative AI platforms are gaining popularity and more applications are being discovered, these technologies should not be used as end-to-end creative solutions. Their true power lies in combining AI output with human thought (and hands). While generative AI is revolutionary, like the internet or mobile phone, there’s still a strong need for human judgment.
The next creative revolution is here if you know how to incorporate generative AI into your existing marketing workflows. Here’s how you can embrace generative AI and enhance your overall marketing efforts.
Use It As A Tool
Look around and you’ll find any number of articles about how AI will replace jobs. Generative AI is really good at baseline tasks as well as providing a starting point for creative refinement. What it is not good at is mastering someone’s job.
The best marketers use generative AI as a tool, just like their CMS system or their SEO platform. It can help uncover insights and help you build on current themes or ideas.
Using AI strategically as part of projects can help enhance your output and increase your productivity. But with any good tool, its output needs a critical eye and a human touch. Protecting copyright will be a critical need, both for the government and for marketers alike. Pay attention to how the government monitors and treats generative AI tools as you implement them into your processes.
Create More Space For Creativity
Rather than seeing AI as a threat, look to it as a tool that can help you create space for more creativity. You can use ChatGPT or its counterparts for repeatable tasks, ideation and even research, for example. Subject line testing, keyword optimization, drafting ad copy or even writing outlines of articles are also great use cases for generative AI. One HubSpot study found that almost 70% of marketers who use AI are using it to create content faster, and 50% believe it ultimately makes their content better.
The reality is that AI can help you evolve your workflows and innovate processes, enabling your team to work efficiently and effectively while producing better-quality products. When we were first drafting our AI policy, we asked ChatpGPT to create a draft for us. This gave us something to work from before we turned to our subject matter experts in creative, media, analytics and human resources to evaluate what it gave us.
Find The Right Target Audience
Effective marketing depends on the ability to create content your target audience needs when and where they need it. However, generative AI can help you predict new leads and identify larger audiences for outreach.
We’ve tested this approach with customized, pre-made AI models that we use to cluster the best target audiences. The technology can predict the “best customer” and upload Google and Facebook look-alike audience targeting to help us increase our reach.
This level of detail and research would have taken our team hours in the past. Now, we’re able to more efficiently align target audiences with marketing tactics. And we’re not alone. McKinsey & Company found that “at the top of the funnel, gen AI surpasses traditional AI-driven lead identification and targeting that uses web scraping and simple prioritization.”
Respond To Your Customers In A Personalized Way
In a world of fluctuating customer demand, generative AI can help you develop personalized messaging to reach your key demographics. AI can create scalable, customized follow-up emails you can send to clients and prospects. It can also provide on-demand customer service support.
Since AI learns through analyzing customer behavior and data, coupling it with chatbots can give you the ability to respond in real time to customer questions while also providing a rich database of information for future marketing campaigns and initiatives.
However, always remember that there’s power in human connection. Be careful in presenting findings from AI, and make sure you use real spokespeople in your messaging. Humanity is a powerful tool for reaching your customer base.
Generative AI: Your Marketing Companion
At a time when marketing dollars are stretched thin, AI can help drive more effective and efficient results. Look at it as a companion to help you analyze data and make optimized decisions. It allows you to automate more tedious tasks, gives you the ability to rapidly explore new ideas, and inspires new roads of thinking.
Rather than seeing AI as a threat, embrace its power to enhance your overall marketing goals and strategy.

title: Council Post: Remember The Human Element Of The Emerging AI World
text:
Chief Executive Officer at Safeguard Global.
As the newest wave of artificial intelligence applications (and the hype that surrounds them) continues to make its mark in various sectors, one thing is becoming clear: Humans have more of a role to play in the future of AI than naysayers claim. Contrary to popular belief, AI isn't about removing, much less replacing, people. It's about rethinking work, skills and how we continue to evolve human potential.
Using AI doesn’t mean you’re surrendering to a machine. Instead, you're leveraging technology as a means to accomplishing your more laborious tasks. For example, Zendesk implemented a ChatGPT plugin to synthesize customer information and provide AI-generated answers to frequently asked questions. By processing vast amounts of data, AI can reduce time spent on repetitive research tasks, allowing your employees to focus on work that's more complex, requires critical thinking and deserves more sensitive responses.
Humans Create The Quality In AI Relationships
As counterintuitive as it may seem to the AI-fearful, there are many approaches to incorporating this technology effectively into your business. By taking a steady, agile and practical approach, many companies have realized a shift in how their business opportunities merge with or complement the potential of their people. What's vital is to remember that, as powerful as AI is, its output depends on what we put into it.
While it may seem like an old cliche, "garbage in, garbage out" is a concept that still holds true today, especially regarding how we use AI. The quality of AI-generated results is only as good as the data it's fed. That's why confidence in the source material is critical, as is understanding AI's limitations. For instance, ChatGPT doesn't read minds; it processes information based on human-provided prompts that establish the boundaries of a proper, accurate response.
Though we may need fewer people for certain tasks as AI adoption becomes more mainstream, the demand for responsiveness, critical thinking and analytical and creative skills will remain important to organizations. These traits are invaluable for a workforce that wants to harness AI's complementary capabilities.
A New Approach To The Workforce
A stunning 84% of top-tier executives believe leveraging AI is not just beneficial, but inevitable. With the future demanding the integration of these tools, organizations must equip themselves to keep pace with rapid technological advancement.
In the post-industrial era, labor was the driving factor of production, and when an employee couldn’t meet or keep up with the changing needs of their role, they were replaced. But in today’s landscape, companies' responses to the rapid changes in technology are putting more emphasis on employee training and reskilling so top talent can adapt to new technology.
Understand Your Company's Current Skills Composition
Before embracing AI, the first thing you must do is get a clear idea of the skills and capabilities of your workforce. This can comprise current skill sets, training criteria and insights from managers about their people and their potential.
From there, you can begin to look at how to apply AI in your organization by reviewing examples and functions that are currently challenging the old ways of working. While skill sets will need to continue to change, that doesn’t need to come from an entirely new workforce once AI is more fully integrated into work experiences. Instead, you can train the workforce to align with technology's capabilities. For instance, repetition-based tasks may offer higher-level opportunities for interns with a background in data and statistics because they can help compose prompts for document management or searches on existing databases.
Evolve Employees' Skills To Capitalize On AI Tech
Similar to how AI fills the gaps between existing roles, your workforce can adapt to what this technology looks like in practice. The absence of on-the-job training is a missed opportunity for businesses, so ensure you have a skills-forward approach to your workforce strategy. Provide resources and opportunities for employees to learn about AI. They should be able to experiment with tools to understand limitations and learn to review output with a critical eye. This creates a "walk before you run" mindset that's backed by the institutional knowledge of your company.
Encouraging this kind of exploration requires allocating time for employees to experiment with new tools and technology. Additionally, executives should lead by example and learn, share and ask questions about new AI resources. A structured approach to AI adoption that focuses on learning opportunities rather than an assumptive "one size fits all" mindset will be vital to your implementation strategies.
AI is not a replacement for human ingenuity; it's an augmentation. The rise of this technology presents an opportunity for us to rethink work and skills, allowing us to focus on the areas where humans truly excel—creativity, strategic thinking and understanding complex emotions. The AI world is a people-dependent one, where its true benefit is in how it’s used.

title: Council Post: Beware Of Artificial Intelligence With Puppy Dog Eyes
text:
As Q2's Chief Technology Officer, Adam Blue drives the overarching innovation strategy to solve current and future customer challenges.
The other night, as I re-watched WALL-E, I thought about how prescient the 2008 film was in foreseeing issues around artificial intelligence and what can happen when humans become reliant on technology. It tells the story of a lone trash compactor (WALL-E) left on an uninhabitable Earth to clean up the trash left behind by humans, who have evacuated to spaceships where they live sedentary lives as blobs staring at screens all day. Even when side by side, they speak through their devices rather than to each other. Sound familiar?
WALL-E takes place in 2805, and because machines have eliminated the need for humans to work, they spend all their time seeking fulfillment through consumerism. At the heart of the movie is a love story between WALL-E and another robot, EVE. In a 2020 interview, screenwriter Andrew Stanton said he wanted to tell a story of a robot with more humanity than humans.
He succeeded. I dare you not to fall in love with WALL-E, who’s basically a trash compactor with a pair of binoculars on top that look remarkably similar to human eyes—and that’s the point. WALL-E works as a character because we’re able to connect with him on an emotional level.
Humans focus on things we can interact with and respond emotionally and empathically. For example, think about our relationship with dogs. Their eyes are expressive because they have eyebrows, and they have eyebrows because they evolved that way as they diverged from wolves—with help from human breeders along the way. Humans love to anthropomorphize things, be it dogs or cute trash compactors.
And this brings us to AI. Because AI is at the point that it can simulate human characteristics, we’re tempted to anthropomorphize it, too. Siri’s not a person, so why does it have a name? It’s to make us feel more comfortable using it—like we aren’t disclosing personal information to a huge conglomerate; we’re simply conversing with a trusted assistant.
It's natural for people to look into the heart of a machine and want to see themselves. Many AI components are impressive to us because they so closely simulate human interaction, and that’s compelling.
But it’s also dangerous. Every technology that tilts the balance of our world toward further inequity of income, opportunity or autonomy does each of us irreparable harm. That doesn’t mean it's “take over the world, and we're all going to end up in the apocalypse'' dangerous. That's probably not going to happen. The negative effects of technology often play out in ways that are radically different than we expected. As a result, we’re not always prepared.
The world wide web, for example, was imagined as a utopian open platform for people to share information and ideas. And while we are able to access almost any fact in a matter of seconds, today’s internet is far from utopian. It’s not only controlled by a few powerful corporations that use data and algorithms to feed content to users but it’s also been weaponized by governments and other bad actors to disseminate false information and propaganda. Unfortunately, there’s no turning back on the unintended consequence of the internet.
Is AI Frankenstein’s Monster?
This notion of technology moving faster than we can manage is critically important, particularly with AI—and that’s where we are. In March, after OpenAI released a new version of ChatGPT, more than a thousand tech leaders signed an open letter urging a halt in the development of new AI technologies because of their “profound risks to society and humanity.” Two months later, AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton resigned from Google and warned of the dangers of generative AI, which is used in ChatGPT. As if those events weren’t startling enough, in mid-May, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman urged Congress to regulate AI, saying his biggest concern was AI’s potential threat to our democracy.
It felt to me as if Altman and other tech pioneers had given a class of third graders a case of Red Bull and a bunch of chainsaws and, as they walked away, casually suggested that some teachers might want to check on the children.
Much like Dr. Frankenstein, who created something he ultimately couldn’t control, industry leaders, by their own admission, don’t fully understand how ChatGPT works. So we have to use ChatGPT cautiously and responsibly—because these powerful tools can get away from us in the same way that Frankenstein’s creation got away from him.
I’m not suggesting that all AI is bad. On the contrary, my company has developed some innovative tools that combine AI with human expertise to combat bank fraud. AI has a place, and it’s going to change the world, but it’s not a panacea. For people in the developing world whose days are filled with trying to obtain clean water or provide basic subsistence for their families, I'm not sure how much AI will do for them.
We’re not going to solve every problem by being smarter or through the use of technology. Our problems will be solved through hard work, cooperation, empathy, humility, debate and a myriad of other ways. In that sense, the assistive use cases for AI are much more interesting than the replacement use cases. But there is a coming shift in which the use of AI will create greater productivity for a lot of people in knowledge work who are used to owning their own productivity.
And this leads us to a fundamental question that arises whenever there's a technological advance: When people get more productive, who owns the surplus? Is there a way to use the surplus created by AI in a way that's meaningful, or will we end up as floating blobs void of humanity staring at screens all day?
Films express the fear and anxiety as well as the excitement and possibility that come with new technology. As WALL-E so beautifully illustrated, until we can train AI to be empathic and until it possesses authentic humanity, it's just a tool.

title: Council Post: Generative AI Magnifies A Crisis In Enterprise IT & Security
text:
Russell is the CEO and founder of Nudge Security, a startup that's redefining the human element of cybersecurity for modern work.
The breakneck speed at which generative AI has mainlined into seemingly every organization this year has caused some major whiplash for enterprise IT, risk and security leaders, who face tough questions about how to govern the use of these new tools without hamstringing the ability to innovate. In practice, many are still struggling to get their arms around the shadow AI being adopted across the organization.
This situation reflects a much larger problem that these leaders have been facing for years. A tectonic shift has taken place in technology adoption in the workplace: Over the last five years, top-down IT procurement has been usurped by business-led and employee-led IT adoption. This shift has made it difficult for technology governance leaders to keep tabs on what tools are being used, where sensitive data resides and who (and what) has access to it.
The difference now is that everyone is paying close attention to the data privacy and security concerns of generative AI in the workplace. Enterprise IT, risk and security leaders are at a pivotal moment. How they address AI governance will have a larger, lasting impact on the perception and influence of their functions within their organizations. Bungle it, and they’ll be invited to go sit in a corner and patch vulnerabilities while the business moves forward without them. Master it, and they’ll have laid the groundwork for a modern, adaptable IT security and governance model that allows the business to move forward quickly and safely.
To balance the risks and potential rewards of these emerging technologies without repeating past mistakes, enterprise IT, risk and security leaders need a new approach to securing and governing access to new cloud-delivered technologies. Here are a few do’s and don’ts to consider.
Don’t Compromise On Visibility
You can’t manage what you can’t see, which is why visibility is a prerequisite for enacting any security policy. Yet, the question, “What SaaS tools are employees actually using?” often lands with a record scratch. The oversight of technology use that IT and security teams once had has steadily eroded against the rising tides of remote work, BYOD and the proliferation of cloud and SaaS applications.
Left to mine DNS records, expense reports and internal Slack channels to cobble together an incomplete picture of unsanctioned SaaS use, IT and security teams lack the context they need to understand what SaaS tools are being adopted and when, by whom, and for what purposes. This context, along with insights into what types of data are being shared, what business systems are being connected and what the vendors’ security profiles and terms of service look like, is essential to assessing organizational risk, making policy decisions and enforcing those policies.
It’s no longer enough to limit IT oversight to a subset of carefully procured enterprise SaaS applications. Rather, IT and security teams must work to gain visibility of the long tail of unsanctioned cloud and SaaS use, even when workers are off-network and on personal devices. The good news is that this is possible—just not with legacy approaches and perimeter-based monitoring technologies. Next-generation SaaS asset discovery solutions exist for today’s hybrid, cloud-first world and are worth considering.
Weigh The Pros And Cons Of Wholesale Bans On AI
Samsung, Apple, Verizon and other major companies made headlines recently for their broad-sweeping restrictions on the use of generative AI tools like ChatGPT. But is that the right approach? Is it even enforceable?
IT and security leaders face a difficult balancing act in governing the adoption and use of emerging cloud and SaaS technologies. As one technology leader put it, there’s “a fear of missing out and a fear of messing up.” Lean too far into allowing experimental SaaS use without safeguards, and you could increase risk, sprawl and operational inefficiencies. Lean too far into blocking unsanctioned SaaS, and you could stifle an organization’s ability to innovate, or more likely, employees will just work around these controls and processes altogether.
The question IT and security organizations should be asking is, “How can we enable safe SaaS use at the speed of business, and what do we need to get there?” For example, instead of delaying SaaS procurement by weeks to conduct vendor security reviews, organizations can work toward just-in-time assessments that run as SaaS applications are adopted, alerting IT and security teams to risky or non-compliant findings.
Don’t Blame Employees For Experimenting
Traditional media and social media have been plastered recently with messages about how learning generative AI is the ultimate productivity hack and a must-have skill set for any modern digital worker. Can you really blame employees for brazenly, if not recklessly, experimenting with these new shiny objects, especially when getting started is as simple as entering a corporate email address, throwing down a few bucks on the company credit card and feeding it work: code, customer data, next month’s earnings report, whatever.
Security awareness training won’t solve this because it isn’t a “stupid user” problem; it’s a conflict of interests. Employees want to skill up, work efficiently and help the business succeed. And, if an IT policy or security control stands in the way of that, most workers will opt to beg for forgiveness rather than ask for permission. According to Gartner, 74% of employees said they would be willing to bypass cybersecurity guidance if it helped them or their team achieve a business objective.
Do Focus On How To Operationalize SaaS Security
So much of the current discussion on AI security has focused on what security policies should look like, yet too little of the discussion has focused on how policies should be (and can be) enacted and enforced. Without the right SaaS security and governance process and technology in place, IT and security leaders risk losing the ability and the right to govern IT going forward. However, with the bright spotlight on generative AI, they can seize the opportunity to address this existential crisis and create a path forward to sustainable technology governance.
