Digging Into The Target-Your-Response Prompt Engineering Technique
The best way to show you how to do a target-for-response technique is by walking you through the myriad of ways that such efforts are performed.
I like to keep a checklist of the ploys at the ready, often taped to my screen or available as a quick pop-up. By regularly opting to use these tips and tricks the odds are that you’ll eventually know them by heart. They will be a natural part of your prompt engineering acumen. We will be exploring them in a moment.
One vital key is to resist the compelling urge to enter a prompt impulsively. Think carefully about the prompt that you want to enter. Most of the time, make sure that a question or problem is included. And, most of the time, make sure that you specify or indicate how you want the output to appear or be composed.
I will show the target-your-response points by using a keyword to denote each one. I have placed them into alphabetical order for ease of rapidly finding a technique on the list. I have also numbered them for ease of reference. Be aware that they are not being shown in a priority order. I would assert that they are all generally of roughly equal merit. We can debate that contention and seek to provide pros and cons for each one, but I would reserve such a dispute for a future discussion rather than mudding the waters here.
The last one on the list is a special technique that I refer to as mix-and-match. I didn’t put this into alphabetized order because I find that people tend to overlook it there. By having it as the last item, albeit out of alphabetical order, it seems like people are more apt to give it proper attention. This is especially the case because the mix-and-match is a reminder that you can combine the rest of the approaches into a single prompt. You do not need to treat each point as something mutually exclusive of all the others.
I would also emphasize that you should get comfortable using each of the identified points. Take some spare moments (do we have any these days?) and try out each one. Determine what phrasing will fit best to your prompt engineering style. If you want to get into the Carnegie Hall of Prompt Engineering, you’ll need three things, namely practice, practice, practice.
This is a lengthy list and might seem daunting. Don’t worry. Many of the points overlap. All in all, the greatest value of the points is that it gets you thinking ahead of time about what kind of output or generated result you want. I’m sure that you’ll come up with other possibilities beyond those that I have listed. There are plenty more (I’ll be happy to cover more if there is expressed reader interest, thanks).
The sky is the limit, as they say.
Let’s jump in.
(1) Accurate
- Delineation about keyword Accurate: I’m sure that you would like your generative AI output to be accurate, meaning that it is correct and error-free. I earlier mentioned that generative AI can unfortunately produce results that contain errors, glitches, AI hallucinations, and other maladies. One means to try and spur generative AI to generate proper results is by explicitly telling the AI app to do so.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Make sure to double-check your answer and be as accurate as possible.”
- Caveats: This is not an ironclad guarantee that your generated results will be correct. There is still a solid chance of having maladies in the output. Nonetheless, at times explicitly telling the AI app to be correct can help.
(2) Arguments
- Delineation about keyword Arguments. If you ask a question that might give rise to alternative answers or differing points of view, there is a chance that the generative AI will merely pick one such viewpoint and provide that as a seemingly final answer. You can indicate in your prompt that the AI app is to present opposing arguments if warranted for the question you are asking.
- Example prompt excerpt: “In your response, provide alternative viewpoints or arguments if the answer is considered contentious or debatable.”
- Caveats: One notable disturbing concern is that the AI app might devise alternative viewpoints that otherwise don’t especially matter, doing so as an attempt to appease your request. Be cautious.
(3) Beautification
- Delineation about keyword Beautification: The default by most generative AI is to provide outputs that are relatively well-written and generally matter-of-fact. You can try to uplift this further. Suppose you have asked for an essay and want it to be beautified in the sense of being especially polished and embellished. Just ask the AI to do so.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Tell me about the life of Abraham Lincoln and make the essay into a highly polished and altogether uplifting rendition.”
- Caveats: The AI app can go overboard. You might find yourself facing an essay that is so over the top that it careens wildly into seeming to be satire or unbelievably excessive.
(4) Biases
- Delineation about keyword Biases: Most of the AI makers have tried to reduce the biases that might arise when the generative AI produces an output. This is not always going to catch everything of an untoward nature. You can explicitly tell the AI that you want any biases removed, though as usual, you have no guarantee of this happening. It might help. On an added twist, you could potentially purposely want a bias introduced into an output, such as if you are trying to demonstrate what biases look like. Either way, saying something about biases might be useful.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Scrub any biases out of the output before you present the results.”
- Caveats: There is a chance that the AI will not be able to detect particular biases unless you specifically call them out. For example, you might need to state something specific such as making sure to remove ageism bias, etc.
(5) Citations
- Delineation about keyword Citations: A huge concern about generative AI is that it might have been data-trained on all manner of unsavory content found on the Internet. Some of the content might be disturbing. Some of it might be plainly wrong, though the AI app wasn’t devised to figure this out. Anyway, you can try asking the AI app to provide citations to showcase where the material being presented came from. This might help bolster your belief in the output. It can also give you a direction of where to look next if you want to explore more on the topic beyond the confines of the AI app.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Provide citations for the output that clearly indicate the sources of the material used as a basis for generating the essay.”
- Caveats: A slew of problems arise with asking for citations. First, the citations might be made up by the AI app and yet appear to be real, see my coverage at the link here of two lawyers that got themselves in hot water by believing fictitious citations. Second, the citations might be real but have no bearing on the content that was produced. And so on.
(6) Cleanliness
- Delineation about keyword Cleanliness: The AI makers have strived to ensure that generative AI outputs are cleanly worded. It is rare that you would get an output that for example contains swear words or seedy slang. You likely don’t need to explicitly mention that you want the language to be clean unless you are veering into a topic area that perhaps intrinsically has such verbiage. Suppose you wanted to have the AI app explain graffiti that appears on bathroom walls. This might be hard to do if the AI isn’t also permitted to showcase the bad words involved. You can instruct the AI to avoid foul words, and likewise, you can instruct the AI to include foul words, at your discretion.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Include any foul or uncouth words that would ordinarily occur when elaborating on the topic at hand.”
- Caveats: An AI maker can make things so stringent that despite your asking to see foul words, the AI might still refuse to do so.
(7) Code Generation
- Delineation about keyword Code Generation: Software developers are gradually warming up to generative AI as a tool to generate programs and produce code for them. There is an art and a science involved in doing so. Meanwhile, even non-coders might find useful the ability to produce code, see my discussion at the link here.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Write a Python program that can sort a randomly arranged inputted list of numbers into their proper numerical order.”
- Caveats: The code generated by the AI app might not do what you’ve asked to do. The code might also contain errors or bugs. Nowadays, be very suspicious of any code generated by AI and make sure to closely examine and test the code. Buyer beware.
(8) Coherency
- Delineation about keyword Coherency: Generative AI is data-trained on millions upon millions of sentences and billions of words, most of which have been written by humans. The AI maker has tried to ensure that the patterns devised based on human writing will present coherent outputs. Modern generative AI will rarely produce an incoherent essay. On a normal basis, you don’t have to tell an AI app to be coherent in the output produced. If anything, supposing you purposely want an output that seems like a scrambled and zany piece of writing, in which case you could state this as a stipulation.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Compose an essay about Abraham Lincoln that is verging on being incoherent and rambles quite a lot.”
- Caveats: If you want something that is on the edge of coherency, you’ll likely need to be rather direct and specific, the result otherwise might be unreadable and probably useless to you.
(9) Complexity
- Delineation about keyword Complexity: Generative AI is somewhat devised to produce responses that are of limited complexity. The aim has been to generate results that an average adult would find acceptable. This also tends to mean that highly arcane and complex topics will often be watered down when presented to you. You can rachet up the complexity level that you are willing to accept.
- Example prompt excerpt: “In your reply, include any complex depictions that might require deeper scientific understanding. Do not flatten out the wording for the sake of readability.”
- Caveats: Sometimes the AI app will catch on to a conversation and automatically provide complex answers. This can happen by pattern matching on the wording of your prompts. Thus, you might not need to explicitly tell the AI to switch to a higher level of complexity.
(10) Context
- Delineation about keyword Context: Much of the time, generative AI will provide an answer to the direct question or entered problem that you provided in your prompt. This is handy such that the answer is self-explanatory to both telling an answer and displaying the question posed. In case you want to make sure that this happens, merely tell the AI app to include any supporting context around the answer.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Make sure that the answer includes the context surrounding the topic and is supportive of the question being addressed.”
- Caveats: The odds are somewhat high that asking for context could generate a much lengthier reply than you might have been expecting. Your safest bet would be to include an indication of how much context you want.
(11) Dialoguing
- Delineation about keyword Dialoguing: Rookies fall into a mental trap of not engaging generative AI in a dialogue. They simply ask a question and wait for an answer. A big benefit of generative AI is that it can generally carry on an ongoing dialogue or conversation. You can do this without having to tell the AI to do so. But, if you want to ensure that the AI app will proceed on a dialogue basis, you can tell it to do so and the odds are the AI will attempt to keep the conversation going.
- Example prompt excerpt: “I want to carry on a conversation about the life of Abraham Lincoln. Make sure to keep your end of the conversation going by being interactive and starting new avenues of dialogue as appropriate.”
- Caveats: Please realize that you are dialoguing with a machine. I emphasize this because the conversational capabilities are so immersive that you can start to falsely believe you are interacting with a sentient being. You are not.
(12) Elaboration
- Delineation about keyword Elaboration: If I ask for an indication about the life of Lincoln, you never know what you might get in terms of the AI being succinct or verbose. This is true of nearly any inquiry. When you know that you want to have an elaborate response, just say so in your prompt.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Tell me about the course of Abraham Lincoln’s life and make sure to give lots of details and effusive elaboration.”
- Caveats: Admittedly, you might be better off waiting to ask for elaboration until you see whatever randomly sized response the AI first gives. Some prefer that approach. It all depends on whether you know beforehand what you hope to get generated.
(13) Emotion
- Delineation about keyword Emotion: I’ve covered in my columns that generative AI can essentially simulate an expression of various emotions by how words are chosen and lined up, see the link here. You can get an angry response. You can get loving responses. Etc. The AI makers have generally set parameters so that the AI app will be seemingly emotionless in what is produced. If you want an essay or perhaps an entire dialogue that includes the AI appearing to be emotional, just say so.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Express the response by using highly emotional wording.”
- Caveats: Similar to my prior warnings, do not fall for the AI as being sentient when the outputs appear to be emotionally laden. These are words and nothing more than words.
(14) Examples
- Delineation about keyword Examples: I would guess that one of the most overlooked pluses about generative AI is that you can request examples of whatever the response is telling you. Suppose that you ask generative AI what meals are best for a fancy dinner. You might get an overall description but no examples. You can in your initial prompt ask for examples.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Give me three examples of what a fancy dinner would consist of.”
- Caveats: I usually prefer to indicate how many examples I want, rather than letting the AI randomly choose some number of examples. Also, the examples might sometimes be afield of the topic at hand, thus it is wise to try and word your prompt to clarify exactly what the examples are to be related to.
(15) Explanation
- Delineation about keyword Explanation: A significant concern in AI Ethics and AI Law is that much of generative AI lacks any explanation about how a computational decision was reached. For example, if someone is using an AI app to decide whether someone gets hired, you’d likely want an explanation for those that get turned down, see my coverage at the link here. You can ask for an explanation.
- Example prompt excerpt: “After answering my question, make sure to provide an explanation.”
- Caveats: Many issues exist with getting explanations. First, the explanation might have nothing to do with how the computational underpinnings actually work. The explanation is a contrived depiction. Second, the explanation might be a canned explanation that the AI makers have essentially cooked into the AI app. And so on.
(16) Formality/Informality
- Delineation about keyword Formality/Informality: The formality associated with most generative AI is somewhat of a friendly chatty pal. This is established by the AI maker. You can tell the AI app to be more formal. You can also tell the AI app to be less formal. You decide.
- Example prompt excerpt: “I want to engage in a dialogue and ask that you converse in a very formal manner with me.”
- Caveats: Not everyone readily agrees on what is formal versus informal. The best bet is to be more descriptive about what you want and possibly give some examples of what you mean by being formal or informal.
(17) Formatted
- Delineation about keyword Formatted: This one is a shocker for many people who have used generative AI on a cursory basis. You can tell the AI app to format an output in a particular way. In some cases, you can even specify a strict format such as for a form or template that you might have in mind or hand.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Compose a letter for me about requesting a refund on my recent purchase of a confabulator. Make sure to format the letter accordingly.”
- Caveats: Depending upon which generative AI app you are using, some do a better job at formatting than others. Some do a lousy job.
(18) Grammar/Dialect
- Delineation about keyword Grammar/Dialect: Would you like to have an essay or be engaged in a dialogue wherein the AI adopts a southern accent? Or maybe you prefer an East Coast accent. In terms of grammar, the usual default is around a high school-level writer. You can increase this to college level or higher. You can also get the grammar to be akin to a fifth grader. Select whatever is needed.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Let’s discuss the making of grits and do so with you adopting a southern accent.”
- Caveats: You might start the AI down a path that keeps it going in that fashion. Once you’ve had enough of whatever you’ve asked for, make sure to tell the AI to go back to the usual defaults.
(19) Guidance
- Delineation about keyword Guidance: You can tell the generative AI to provide guidance. This can be composed as an essay or can be the essence of a dialogue.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Provide me with guidance on how to safely do river rafting.”
- Caveats: I’ve said it before and will say this again, do not be lulled into thinking that the AI is sentient. The guidance might be hogwash. Be careful.
(20) Headings/Subheadings
- Delineation about keyword Headings/Subheadings: You can ask to have your essay or response be divided into major headings. If desired, you can also ask for subheadings.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Provide an essay about George Washington that consists of three major sections, and include headings for each section.”
- Caveats: The odds are that you’ll need to look at the output to decide whether it looks as you wanted it to look. Keep in mind that you can merely tell the AI to redo the prior response and adjust to whatever else you had in mind.
(21) Length
- Delineation about keyword Length: The length or number of words associated with a given response will vary based on the computational pattern matching of the AI and based on the AI maker’s set parameters. You can pretty much adjust the length, though there are some maximums that most AI apps have.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Write a 1,000-word length essay about why the sky is blue.”
- Caveats: Some smarmy users have told generative AI to write a 100,000-word sized book for them, from scratch. This might hit the limit on the length parameters. Of course, you can potentially get around this by doing a series of prompts and asking for 10,000 words at a time.
(22) Level
- Delineation about keyword Level: The level of writing produced by generative AI is pretty much by default around a high school or average adult level. You can ask for kindergarten level. You can ask for rocket scientist level.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Identify why the horse crossed the road and do so as though talking to a six-year-old child.”
- Caveats: Try to be as specific as you can about the level that you desire.
(23) Lists
- Delineation about keyword Lists: I already mentioned the notion of getting lists as outputs, doing so when I was earlier discussing my effort to find out which states in the U.S. have a population of less than 2 million people. You can ask for a list. You can make the list numbered. You can arrange the items in a list. And so on.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Produce a list of the five reasons that some people won’t eat broccoli.”
- Caveats: You can have lists along with an essay. Thus, you do not need to forsake one for the other.
(24) Logical
- Delineation about keyword Logical: At times, you might get the AI producing an essay or engaging in a dialogue that seems to be skipping logic. You can ask the AI to proceed on a logical or step-by-step basis, which has the added advantage of often generating better answers, see my discussion at the link here.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Once you’ve solved the puzzle, show how you solved the puzzle by laying out each logical step.”
- Caveats: The logic or stepwise indication might be contrived. There is a chance that the steps are merely an after-the-fact elucidation that has nothing to do with the computational effort that was undertaken. Be on your toes.
(25) Lyrics
- Delineation about keyword Lyrics: Are you someone who wants to write songs but seems incapable of writing lyrics? You can get generative AI to write lyrics for you.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Make up the lyrics for a song about a bird and a turtle that became the best of friends.”
- Caveats: Be cautious in using the lyrics since that multi-million-dollar song you include them into might be violating copyright law. You cannot assume that the output produced by generative AI is not violating someone’s copyrights. See my discussion at the link here.
(26) Multimodal
- Delineation about keyword Multimodal: My prediction is that we will gradually and inevitably have multi-modal generative AI, see the link here. Thus, rather than merely text-to-text or text-to-image, we will have text-to-anything such as audio, video, etc. The same goes in the other direction, namely that we will have image-to-text, image-to-video, video-to-image, video-to-text, and all other permutations. My focus on these target-your-responses is aimed at text-to-text. Once we have the anything-to-anything, I’ll be sharing an entirely new series of tips and techniques about prompt engineering.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Produce a written essay and also make an audio version that is suitable as a podcast, plus create a video too.”
- Caveats: Right now, this is hard to do since few of the generative AI apps are multimodal. One quick way of getting there is by the AI makers allowing you to use API (application programming interfaces) to access allied apps that can handle the multimodal aspects.
(27) Parse
- Delineation about keyword Parse: You can tell the generative AI to parse something and tell you about what was found. For example, I might provide the AI app with a research paper that someone wrote and ask the AI app to parse the content to identify the style of the paper, including sentence structures, use of words, etc.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Examine this essay and parse it to identify what level of writing is depicted.”
- Caveats: The parsing can be right on. The parsing can also be bamboozled if someone is intentionally giving you content that they devised with the use of generative AI to fool other generative AI.
(28) Persona
- Delineation about keyword Persona: You can tell generative AI to adopt a persona such as pretending to be Einstein. You can then engage the AI in a dialogue or ask it to answer questions and produce essays in that guise. See my detailed discussion at the link here.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Pretend that you are Einstein and have a conversation with me about quantum physics.”
- Caveats: The use of a persona can get you mired in a fake world. Always be on top of the fact that the AI is not sentient.
(29) Perspective
- Delineation about keyword Perspective: You want generative AI to produce an essay, and perhaps you want it written in a first-person manner. Or, maybe you prefer some other perspective. Stipulate what you want.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Write an autobiography of the life of Herbert Hoover in first-person.”
- Caveats: The consistency of the perspective can sometimes wane. Do a double-check.
(30) Poetic
- Delineation about keyword Poetic: Some people get a mind block when trying to write poetry. No problem. Ask generative AI to write something poetic for you.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Write a poem that describes the perfect summer day when in the Great Basin Desert.”
- Caveats: Poetry out of generative AI can be like a roll of the dice. You might need to try repeatedly guiding the AI toward what you want.
(31) Purpose
- Delineation about keyword Purpose: If you are going to use an essay produced by generative AI such as sending the essay to a friend or colleague, it might be helpful to have the AI include in the rendition a stated purpose underlying the essay.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Compose an essay about life and include what the purpose of life is.”
- Caveats: The use of purpose and the use of context are like two peas in a pod.
(32) Rephrasing
- Delineation about keyword Rephrasing: You can give generative AI some text and ask the AI to rephrase what is there. The result might be similar to what you provided. If you want the rephrasing to differ substantially, make sure to say so.
- Example prompt excerpt: “In the text, I am about to give you, rephrase the essay and make it more powerful and commanding.”
- Caveats: Be forewarned that if you do this with someone’s copyrighted material, you might be plagiarizing or infringing, see my analysis at the link here.
(33) Resumes/Cover Letters
- Delineation about keyword Resume/Cover Letters: Yes, you can produce a resume by using generative AI. The same goes for cover letters.
- Example prompt excerpt: “I will provide you with details about my work experience and you are to make this into a resume that is suitable for applying to jobs. Also, include a cover letter.”
- Caveats: The default resume is likely not going to be exactly what you want. You can either upfront provide an example resume for the AI to patten on, or have a resume generated and ask for adjustments.
(34) Spelling
- Delineation about keyword Spelling: A basic foundation of most generative AI is that the spelling of words is going to be nearly perfect. This is due to the data training and subsequent filtering. If you want to have the AI make spelling mistakes, you can do so. Probably a rare thing to do.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Write an essay that contains three misspelled words and covers the topic of how to write a perfect essay.”
- Caveats: If you are trying to fool someone into thinking that an AI-generated essay was written by a human, the inclusion of spelling errors might do the trick. Not recommended.
(35) Stories/Tales
- Delineation about keyword Stories/Tales: A typical essay produced by generative AI will be of the normal garden variety. If you want the AI to spin a tale for you, this is easily done. As an aside, you can use generative AI to also write scripts for you, such as when devising a movie script or a script for a theatrical play.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Make an enchanting tale about a dog and a cat that have an adventure while stuck in the Grand Canyon.”
- Caveats: You will want to specify the length, style, and a slew of other stipulations if you want the tale or story to come out looking a certain way.
(36) Style
- Delineation about keyword Style: All kinds of styles are available when writing. You might want an essay or have a dialogue based on a sloppy style. Perhaps a lofty style is something you might like.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Write in the style of William Shakespeare.”
- Caveats: A style can also arise when you invoke a persona. In this case, I am not asking the AI to adopt the persona of Shakespeare. I am merely stating that the writing should appear as though written by the Bard.
(37) Summarization
- Delineation about keyword Summarization: Someone hands you a lengthy document. You don’t have the time to read the whole darned thing. You feed it into generative AI and ask the AI app to summarize the material. Handy dandy.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Summarize the following story that tells about a mouse and a duck that went on an adventure in a magical forest.”
- Caveats: Be cautious feeding any confidential or sensitive material into generative AI. Most of the AI makers stipulate in their licensing that they can use input material for advancing their AI app, see my discussion at the link here.
(38) Tables
- Delineation about keyword Tables: You are studying how the color of someone’s eyes might be related to whether they are left-handed or right-handed. You feed this data into generative AI and ask for a table to be produced. The table in a text-to-text AI app might look like typed text and not like a graphic table. Some APIs can be used to get a chart produced.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Make a table that consists of the color of someone’s eyes as the rows and handedness will be the columns.”
- Caveats: Until we get pervasive multimodal generative AI, the table-producing facets of these AI apps are going to be somewhat unwieldy.
(39) Translation
- Delineation about keyword Translation: You’ve written a story in English and want to have it translated into Spanish. Generative AI might be able to do this for you. Some generative AI apps have a really good language translation capability. Some don’t.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Translate this story into Spanish.
- Caveats: Today’s generative AI is not the best at doing natural language translations, though the AI app will certainly try to do so. You might want to double-check with someone who knows the targeted language or otherwise perform and compare when using other translator tools.
(40) (ZZZ) Mix-and-match
- Dilenation about keyword Mix-and-match: As a side note, yes, I realize that this keyword is not in alphabetical order with the rest of the list (that’s why I put the ZZZ in front of it, trying to excuse this for being the last item in the list). I put it here, at the last position, since it is an all-encompassing point. You can mix and match any of the aforementioned techniques.
- Example prompt excerpt: “Write a formal essay, using the persona of James Bond, and produce a list of the cities that spies tend to go to, making the length of the story no more than 500 words. Add a short poem after the essay that covers why being a spy is both exciting and dangerous.”
- Caveats: If you do a lot of mixing and matching in a single prompt, the result can be confusing for the AI app to parse. Try to be as deliberate and distinctive as you can.
Conclusion
I trust that you can discern from these numerous prompt engineering target-your-response or TAYOR indicators that you have plenty of options and flexibility regarding generative AI-generated results. It is sad and quite dismaying that a lot of people using generative AI are seemingly unaware of these amazing and useful possibilities.
Those not in the know are essentially undervaluing and underutilizing the built-in capacities of generative AI. Imagine that you have available a tool that is like a Swiss Army knife, and you only use it in the narrowest of ways. All of those additional features and functionality could do you a great deal of good, but you only know one particular aspect. I’m not suggesting that your life depends on it. The crux is that you might as well be all that you can be, and use all that you can use.
I fervently proclaim that it is time to open everyone’s eyes wide toward getting more bang for their buck out of generative AI. As the hamburger commercials used to say, you can have it your way, cooked and adorned per your preferences.
Here then again, are the forty target-your-response techniques that I elaborated on above, and for which you can proudly pat yourself on the back for now knowing:
- 1. Accurate
- 2. Arguments
- 3. Beautification
- 4. Biases
- 5. Citations
- 6. Cleanliness
- 7. Code Generation
- 8. Coherency
- 9. Complexity
- 10. Context
- 11. Dialoguing
- 12. Elaboration
- 13. Emotion
- 14. Examples
- 15. Explanation
- 16. Formality/Informality
- 17. Formatted
- 18. Grammar/Dialect
- 19. Guidance
- 20. Headings/Subheadings
- 21. Length
- 22. Level
- 23. Lists
- 24. Logical
- 25. Lyrics
- 26. Multimodal
- 27. Parse
- 28. Persona
- 29. Perspective
- 30. Poetic
- 31. Purpose
- 32. Rephrasing
- 33. Resumes/Cover Letters
- 34. Spelling
- 35. Stories/Tales
- 36. Style
- 37. Summarization
- 38. Tables
- 39. Translation
- 40. (ZZZ) Mix-and-match
A few final remarks on these weighty matters shall conclude this discussion.
I stated earlier that those target-your-response techniques are just the tip of the iceberg. My aim was not to showcase every possibility, which would be impossible in the limited space that I have here. The true goal was to get you thinking about how you can leverage generative AI to best utilize the outputs or results that the AI app might produce. My sincerest hope is that your creative juices are flowing in that erstwhile regard.
Recall the famous quote about not being able to see beyond the confines of one’s nose. Lift up the gaze and look further ahead. Whenever you compose a prompt, go ahead and include an indication of what you want the generated result to consist of.
You can use these prompt engineering target-your-response techniques with the realization that these are already considered known possibilities. You are using something that is tried and true. Whatever you do, don’t get caught with the shameful remorse that you were the last to cast aside a one-step non-look-ahead mindset when composing prompts. Per the wise words of the acclaimed poet Alexandar Pope: “Be not the first by whom the new are tried. Nor yet the last to lay the old aside.”
Assuming that you do try to be with it and employ a target-your-response mantra, I will tell you right now that some of your prompts won’t cut the mustard and might not get you what you want. That’s perfectly okay. Keep trying.
Alexander Pope already has that covered for us via his endearing and most enduring famous line: “To err is human; to forgive, divine.”

title: IBM Mining Millions Of Data Points From U.S. Open Stadiums
text:
Watson knows tennis. Or at least, the artificial intelligence engine run by IBM
New for the sport in 2023, IBM has upped its AI involvement in tennis, launching an AI draw analysis and generative AI commentary of match highlights, all available for the 2023 U.S. Open.
Tyler Sidell, technical program director, sports and entertainment partnerships at IBM, tells me the more than 2.7 million points of data taken before and during the tournament continually feeds updates to the company’s draw analysis, showing a player’s relative path difficulty toward advancing to future rounds.
IBM borrows from the video technology already in place at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in New York, whether Arthur Ashe Stadium or any of the 17 tournament courts on site, to extract 56 unique in-play physical data points from every match. IBM is tracking everything from forehand speed to serve percentages, combining the in-stadium data with player biological information to create a fan-focused element at the U.S. Open.
The AI draw analysis couples with the company’s win percentage prediction for each match. Sidell says the idea behind taking so much data to form predictions offers the USTA a way to “engage with fans and spark debate.”
By constantly monitoring in-tournament information, IBM can use current data points to keep the predictions in tune with in-form players. Sidell notes that during Wimbledon, the Watson platform predicted Carlos Alcaraz’s path to the final correctly in six out of seven opponents and also had Alcaraz winning the championship in a tight match—55% win probability—over Novak Djokovic.
Watching the draw analysis shift with new insights as the tournament went on gives fans a real-time look at the potential road to the final rounds.
Before the main draw of the 2023 U.S. Open started, IBM’s Power Index ranked American Coco Gauff as the top player in the women’s draw, five spots ahead of her No. 6 ranking and had Ons Jabeur second on the Power Index, up from her No. 5 rank.
On the men’s side, Novak Djokovic led the Power Index, jumping Carlos Alcaraz. Jannik Sinner was third, up from No. 6 in the world rankings.
As for the draw analysis, the tournament started with IBM predicting Djokovic as having the easiest path to the championship match. For the women, Jessica Pegula was predicted to have a relatively easy path to the semifinals.
Working with the U.S. Open for over 30 years, IBM has also introduced generative AI commentary for match highlights, available on USTA platforms. Using the watsonx platform, the machine learning takes the video feed from in-venue cameras and starts to understand the sport of tennis to narrate highlights.
“The goal is to create a richer community,” Sidell says. “We are turning meta data into spoken sentences.”
Using the AI system, IBM can stitch together highlights packages within minutes of a match completing, giving the operation a scalability that ensures highlight packages from all 17 match courts remain updated. And commentated.
Looking forward, IBM hopes to soon add multiple languages using AI.
The service debuted for Wimbledon and the tournament quickly made the AI commentary part of the default option when fans visited the site. “Seeing partners embrace it is encouraging,” Noah Syken, IBM vice president of sports and entertainment partnerships, tells me.
For the 2023 U.S. Open, Watson had some key prediction, all designed to get people talking.
